etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 御(お) (o-) + 姉(ねえ) (nē) + さん (-san)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 礼(れい) (rei, “bow”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
*/sam/ → /samu/ → /saɴ/
From Middle Chinese 三 (MC sam|samH). Compare modern Mandarin 三 (sān), literary Hokkien 三 (sam), Cantonese 三 (saam1).
In Old Japanese, this kanji was used phonetically to transcribe さむ (samu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Borrowing from Mandarin 三 (sān), with the pitch accent different from etymology 1. (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
⟨mi1⟩ → /mi/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mi.
Likely an apophonic form of 六 (mu, “six”), compare 四 (yo, “four”) with 八 (ya, “eight”). (Can this(+) etymology be sourced?)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
/mi/ → /miː/
Shift from mi above.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Imperative (命(めい)令(れい)形(けい) (meireikei)) form of 下(くだ)さる (kudasaru, “to give”), the honorific form of 呉(く)れる (kureru). This form is said to have either directly shifted from an earlier 下(くだ)され (kudasare), which is more typical of 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō, “quadrigrade inflection”) and its descendant 五(ご)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (godan katsuyō, “quintigrade inflection”), or to be a clipping of 下(くだ)さいまし (kudasaimashi) or 下(くだ)さいませ (kudasaimase), from 下(くだ)さり (kudasari, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 下(くだ)さる (kudasaru), then shifting from kudasari to kudasai in a process called イ音(おん)便(びん) (i-onbin, “-i sound shift”)) + まし (-mashi) or ませ (-mase), imperative forms of ます (-masu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 二 (nyijH, “two”). Compare modern Northern Min 二 (nī).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
Originally /huta/: *[puta] > [ɸuta]. The ablaut form of 一 (hito2, “one”), which it doubles.
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *puta. Cognate with Japanese 双(ふた) (futa).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Mandarin 两 (liǎng, “two”) with spelling from Mandarin 二 (èr, “two”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨idu⟩ → /id͡zu/ → /d͡zu/ → /d͡zuru/ → /deru/
From Old Japanese 出づ (idu), from Proto-Japonic *intu.
The initial i fell out in compounds where the preceding element ended in i. The du form on its own was not used much outside of compounds until the Kamakura period.
The ending then shifted from -duru (modern -dzuru) to -deru, a shift common to all 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs that occurred from the late Muromachi period through the early Edo period.
Some sources trace the development instead as ⟨idu⟩ → ⟨iduru⟩ → /id͡zuru/ → /d͡zuru/ → /deru/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, ultimately from Proto-Japonic *tikara. Compound of Old Japanese elements 霊 (chi, “power, life force, essence”) +‎ 柄 (kara, “source, origin”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 力 (lik). The goon reading, so likely the initial borrowing. Compare modern Cantonese reading lik6.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 力 (lì), but apparently from a different source dialect or at a different time than 力 (lik). The kan'on reading, so likely a later borrowing. Compare reconstructed Middle Chinese reading /li̯ək/ or Korean reading ryeok.
Only found in compounds and idioms in modern Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨onazi⟩ → /onaʑi/
From Old Japanese.
An irregular adjective even in Classical Japanese (where the attributive form was usually 同じ), it has become more irregular in the modern language, mixing attributes of -i adjectives and -na adjectives (and sometimes neither).
(This etymology is missing or incomplete. Please add to it, or discuss it at the Etymology scriptorium. Particularly: “explain shift from -shiku to -nari to no conjugation needed.”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/onaʑi/ → /onːaʑi/
Long-pronounced form of onaji above.
Compare 南 (minami → minnami, “south”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: The 未(み)然(ぜん)形(けい) (mizenkei, “irrealis”) and 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative”) form of two verb forms of the Sino-Xenic morpheme 同(どう) (dō, “same”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki of 712, the Nihon Shoki completed in 720, and the Man'yōshū completed some time after 759. Perhaps related to Middle Chinese 郡 (MC gjunH, “geographic region: commandery, prefecture”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 國 (MC kwok, “country, nation”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 變 (MC pjenH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Derived from 引(ひ)く (hiku, “to pull”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Compound of 彼 (ka, “that, yon”) +‎ れ (-re, nominalizing suffix for demonstratives). Found in the Man'yōshū compiled around 759.
The sense development seems to have proceeded from "that thing over there" to "that person over there [of indeterminate gender]". The specifically male sense of "he" only arose later during the late Edo period and early Meiji period, influenced by translations of texts from European languages.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: (This term, 彼, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the native Japanese word 心(こころ)配(くば)り (kokorokubari). Can be analyzed as 心(しん) (shin, “heart”) + 配(はい) (hai, “to concern oneself with”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *tay. Compare 目 (me, ma-, “eye”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 手 (MC syuwX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. Ultimately from Proto-Japonic *mətu.
Cognates
Cognate with Kikai 持ちゅい (muchui), Kunigami 持ちゅん (muchun), Northern Amami Ōshima 持と゚ぅり (muθuri), Okinawan 持ちゅん (muchun), Okinoerabu 持ちゅん (muchun), Southern Amami Ōshima 持ちゅむっ (muchum), Tokunoshima 持つぃ (mutsï), Yoron 持ちゅん (muchun), Miyako 持つぃ (mutsï), Yaeyama 持つん (mutsun), and Yonaguni 持とぅん (mutun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 晚 (MC mjonX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 晴(は)れる (hareru, “to be clear (of weather)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From 毎(まい) (mai-, “every”) + 朝(あさ) (asa, “morning”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 毎(まい) (mai-, “every”) + 朝(ちょう) (chō, “morning”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 準備 (MC tsywinX|tsywet bijH). Attested from the early 1800s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The adverbial -く (-ku) form of adjective 無い (nai, “not, missing, not present”) + verb なる (naru, “to become”): literally, "to become not, to become nonexistent".
Cognate with 亡(な)くなる (naku naru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 甘(あま)し (amashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE. From Proto-Japonic *ama.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 甘い, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
⟨woto2ko1⟩ → */wotəkʷo/ → /wotoko/ → /otoko/
From Old Japanese.
Derived from おと (oto, “young?”, cognate with Old Japanese 復つ (wotu → otsu, “to become young again”)) + 子(こ) (ko, “child”).
Compare 少(おと)女(め) (otome, “young woman”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/wo/ → /o/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text: Compound of 男 (o, “male”, see above) +‎ の (no, possessive particle) +‎ 子 (ko, “child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
/nam/ → /namʉ/ → /naɴ/
From Middle Chinese 男 (MC nom).
The 呉音 (goon) reading, so likely the initial borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
etymologies.text:
/dam/ → /damʉ/ → /daɴ/
From Middle Chinese 男 (MC nom).
The 漢音 (kan'on) reading, so likely a later borrowing.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, first attested in the Kojiki (712 CE).
Derived from 斎 (i-, prefix expressing sacredness) + 宣る (noru, “to say or express an intention, usually to a deity”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 細(ふぉそ)し (fososhi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: (This term, 細い, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From classical 四(よ)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (yodan katsuyō) verb 行(おこな)ふ (okonafu), possibly formed from おこ (oko, from 起(お)く (oku)) + なふ (nafu, verb-forming suffix). However, the suffix なふ (-nafu) usually attaches on nominal roots, not other verb stems, making the theorized suffixation unusual.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *aka.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
A repurposing of older term 辞書 (jisho, “letter of resignation”) (see below), based on a reanalysis of the constituent characters 辞 (ji, “resignation, quitting; word”) + 書 (sho, “writing, record, document, book”). Influenced by Middle Chinese-derived term 辞典 (jiten, “dictionary”), wherein the 辞 character expresses the meaning word from Middle Chinese 辭 / 辞 (zi), instead of the meaning resignation or quitting from Middle Chinese 辤 (zi). Note that both of these older character forms were later conflated in both Japanese and Chinese into the simplified version 辞, with the word meaning becoming dominant in Chinese.
First appearance in Japanese with the dictionary sense might be the 1595 publication by the Jesuits of the 羅葡日辞書 (Ra-Ho-Nichi Jisho, “Latin-Portuguese-Japanese Dictionary”), alternate title Dictionarium Latino Lusitanicum, ac Iaponicum.
Compare modern Mandarin 辭書 / 辞书 (císhū, “dictionary, lexicon”), possibly reborrowed from or otherwise influenced by the Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 辤書 / 辤书 (zi syo, literally “quit + writing”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
The 直音表記 (chokuon hyōki, literally “straight-sound spelling”) of jisho above. Most common from the Heian through the Muromachi periods.
It is unclear if the pronunciation itself also shifted, or just the spelling.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1 2
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 零 (MC leng) with an original meaning of a small rainfall.
For the modern sense of zero used since 1248 by mathematician Li Ye, see the Etymology section for Chinese for details.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *tənpu. Cognate with Okinawan 飛ぶん (tubun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Old Japanese. Possibly a verbalization of na-, the 被(ひ)覆(ふく)形(けい) (hifukukei, “bound form”) of 音(ね) (ne, “sound”).
